approvedAsIs.name: Common chickweed
reasons: Lookalike coverage is complete for the real hazards. The two canonical Stellaria media confusions are both present and correctly ranked: scarlet pimpernel / 'poison chickweed' (Lysimachia arvensis, deadly) and the spurges (Euphorbia peplus/helioscopia/maculata, toxic). Poison hemlock is included not as a leaf twin but as the realistic failure mode - a first-year rosette sitting at chickweed height in the same moist disturbed ground, sheared into the same handful. Mouse-ear chickweed is correctly flagged unpalatable, not dangerous. I checked for omitted deadly candidates in the same mat-forming, moist-shade, cool-season niche (lesser celandine, buttercup seedlings, corn spurry, speedwell, pearlwort, Drymaria, nightshade seedlings) and found none that a beginner would plausibly cut into a chickweed handful and that is deadly. Nothing blocking is missing.

Every tell works on the part and in the season actually harvested. The harvest is tender flowerless top growth in the cool season, and the pimpernel tell is deliberately vegetative - square vs round stem, chickweed's single line of non-glandular hairs switching sides at each node, sessile dotted pimpernel leaves vs chickweed's stalked lower leaves - with an explicit instruction NOT to decide on flowers, plus the correct reason (UC IPM: pimpernel flowers stay shut in cool or cloudy weather, which is chickweed's entire season, and young plants have none). That is exactly the failure mode I was looking for and the entry pre-empts it. The spurge test (milky latex vs clear sap) is season- and part-independent, and it correctly warns off leaf arrangement as a spurge tell since petty spurge goes opposite up the stem. The hemlock tell (simple opposite entire leaves on a solid round stem and no smell, vs pinnately compound fern-like alternate basal leaves, musty-mousy crush, hollow purple-blotched stem) is decisive on a rosette.

Caution level matches the risk. 'expert' is correct under the schema definition - deadly lookalikes exist (poison hemlock unambiguously; pimpernel rated deadly is the conservative direction, and the entry is honest that the evidence is livestock fatalities plus a UC IPM range rather than overclaiming human deaths).

Preparation guidance is adequate and specific where it needs to be. Chickweed requires no mandatory detox step, and the entry does not invent one; it names the two real chemical issues with the right magnitude - saponins (poorly absorbed, degraded by thorough cooking, GI upset from a large raw single dose such as a whole batch of pesto) and nitrate accumulation (keep bulk raw servings from infants and small children; avoid heavily fertilised lawns, manure and compost heaps, sprayed beds, roadsides, dog runs). The harvest procedure is procedurally specific rather than vague: clear non-chickweed out of the mat first, shear an inch above ground, then sort the cut handful flat before it goes near a blender.
Schema-valid: all 12 fields present, caution 'expert', danger values all from the allowed set, months all integers 0-11, regions and terrain all legal ids.

NON-BLOCKING - regions are under-inclusive. Stellaria media is recorded in effectively every US state, and the habitat text itself says midwinter is the peak 'in the South', yet 'southcentral' and 'mountain' are omitted. This hides the entry from foragers in TX/OK and the Interior West rather than sending anyone to the wrong place, so it is an accuracy gap, not a safety defect. Worth adding both.

NON-BLOCKING - months exclude July and August (6, 7), which is defensible for a cool-season annual with an 86F germination ceiling, but it contradicts the habitat sentence promising 'near year-round picking in the maritime Northwest'. Again under-inclusive, so not hazardous.

NON-BLOCKING - terrain includes 'woodland' (closed-canopy forest floor is more Stellaria pubera territory than S. media) and omits 'wetland' despite the habitat naming streamside flats and ditch margins. Cosmetic; neither error puts anyone on ground where the risk profile changes.

NON-BLOCKING - 'compost heaps' appears in habitat as a place it grows and again in harvest as a place not to pick from. Internally consistent, but a skimming reader could take the habitat mention as an endorsement; consider marking it as grows-here-don't-eat-here at first mention.

approvedAsIs.name: Dandelion
reasons: Lookalike coverage is complete for the parts and seasons actually harvested. All four pyrrolizidine-alkaloid Senecioneae that share dandelion's ground and rosette window are present (common groundsel, tansy ragwort, coltsfoot, butterweed/cressleaf groundsel), plus the three latex-bearing confusables that the sap test cannot separate (hairy cat's ear, sow thistle, prickly lettuce). I could not identify a missing toxic or deadly mimic: hawkweed, hawkbit, hawksbeard, nipplewort, Agoseris and chicory are all non-toxic, and no acutely lethal dandelion lookalike is established in North America.

caution: "care" is correct under the schema, not under-cautious. No lookalike carries danger "deadly", and the serious ones (Senecio/Jacobaea/Packera/Tussilago) cause cumulative, dose-dependent liver injury rather than single-meal lethality — which the entry states explicitly ("repeated small amounts over weeks or months are the real danger, not a single leaf") rather than hiding. Raising to "expert" would not be supported by any lookalike marked deadly, so the caution/lookalike pair is internally consistent.

The load-bearing tell works on the part and stage actually picked. Milky latex is present in the unbolted rosette leaf and crown — the spring/autumn greens harvest — and Senecio, Jacobaea, Packera and Tussilago are all non-laticiferous, so the test does the work exactly where the flower is absent. Crucially it is stated one-directionally and in the safe direction: no latex rules dandelion OUT, latex does NOT rule it in. Each toxic lookalike's tell also carries rosette-stage backup marks (rounded/blunt crumpled lobes and fleshy or cobwebby texture vs. dandelion's sharp backward-pointing triangular lobes and hairless rosette), so the identification does not rest on sap alone.

NOTE, not blocking — one tell is stage-mismatched: the parts field says "Confirm with the flower stalk" immediately after warning that latex proves nothing, but there is no scape during the pre-bolt greens harvest that the same paragraph calls the best window. This is not safety-bearing because everything the scape test rules out (cat's ear, sow thistle, wild lettuce, chicory) is edible or merely unpalatable, while every toxic lookalike is already excluded by the sap test plus the leaf marks given per-lookalike. Reword to make clear the scape is the confirmation for the flower/petal harvest and the leaf-shape marks are the confirmation for the rosette harvest.

No required safety preparation is omitted — dandelion needs none, and every instruction that could have been vague is specific instead: remove the green base from petals, roots dug early spring or late autumn from plants at least a year old, wash in several changes of water, skip roadsides/ditches/sidewalk cracks entirely (correctly noted as double duty, since that is also where coltsfoot, groundsel and ragwort are thickest). Health contraindications are specific too: taraxinic-acid contact dermatitis, Asteraceae/latex allergy, genuine diuretic effect, and avoid root preparations with gallstones or bile-duct problems.

Schema-valid: all required fields present, no extra keys, months are integers 0-11, regions and terrain values are all legal, caution is a legal literal, and every lookalike has exactly name/danger/tell with legal danger values.

NOTE, not blocking — regions is under-inclusive and contradicts the entry's own text. It lists midwest/northeast/southeast/west but the habitat field says "recorded in all fifty states" (citing USDA FEIS) and the parts field describes harvest windows for "the Southwest" and "interior Northwest", i.e. southcentral and mountain. This should be ["all"]. Every other entry in corrected-pass1.json omits southcentral and mountain identically, so it reads as a corpus-wide convention rather than a dandelion-specific error, and it under-includes rather than misdirects — no one is sent out at a wrong time or place, the entry simply fails to appear for Texas or Rocky Mountain readers.

NOTE, not blocking — months [0,1,2,3,4,8,9,10,11] are correctly 0-indexed and match the described windows (Dec-Mar in the Southeast, Mar-May and Oct-Nov farther north, summer excluded because bolted greens turn bitter), except month 8 (September), which falls outside both windows the parts field states. Harmless over-inclusion — early-autumn regrowth and root digging — but the text and the array should agree.

NOTE, not blocking — the collapsed row renders lead(habitat), whose first sentence advertises "waste ground and sidewalk cracks" as habitat, while the harvest field correctly says to skip sidewalk cracks and roadsides entirely over herbicide, road-salt, dog-traffic and urban-lead contamination. A skimmer who never opens the row sees only the invitation. Consider moving the contamination caveat earlier or softening the habitat lead.

approvedAsIs.name: Ostrich fern fiddleheads
reasons: No missing deadly lookalike. The five listed (lady fern, Dryopteris/male fern, bracken, cinnamon+interrupted fern, sensitive fern) cover every fern crozier sharing spring floodplain habitat. No fern lookalike to ostrich fern in North America is lethal at food quantities, so nothing warrants a 'deadly' entry.

caution: 'care' is correct per the schema definition ('expert' = a deadly lookalike exists). Male fern is the worst case and the entry is honest that recorded fatalities came from concentrated male-fern anthelmintic preparations, not from eating croziers. Consistent with the rest of the corpus, where 'expert' is reserved for entries carrying an actual deadly lookalike.
Every tell is a crozier-stage tell, matched to the part and season actually harvested — no tell that only works on a mature frond or a fertile structure the picker will not have.

The entry does not oversell its own field marks, which is the main way fiddlehead guides get people hurt. It states explicitly that lady fern shares BOTH the papery scales and the U-groove, that scales shed as the crozier elongates so the groove must carry the weight, and (citing NC State on male fern's 'orange-brown scales') that scales alone never confirm ostrich fern. It also warns single lady ferns stand inside ostrich colonies, so nearby fertile plumes never license clearing a patch.

The fuzz-versus-scales reject rule correctly excludes the two woolly genera (Osmundastrum/Osmunda) and bracken's silvery hair, and the groove plus scale-form plus habitat contrast correctly separates Dryopteris (narrow scales persisting up the stalk, round stem, rocky/limy slopes and swamp hummocks, twice-cut frond).

Required safety preparation is present and specific, not vague: rub scales off dry, wash in several changes of cold potable water (never stream water), BOIL at least 15 min or steam 10-12 min with a lid, discard that water and do not reuse it. Sauteing, stir-frying and microwaving are named as NOT adequate cooking, which is exactly the failure mode in the CDC/Health Canada outbreaks the entry cites (MMWR 43(37), 1994, PMID 8078456 verified as a real citation).
Storage and preservation hazards are handled: refrigerate and use within about a week, no oil-packing without acidification (botulism), no pressure canning because no research-tested process exists.

months [3,4,5] = April/May/June is correct for northeast and midwest and matches UMaine's late-April-to-early-June season. The 0-indexed convention is confirmed against sibling entries (Ramps [2,3,4] = Mar-May, Morel [1..6] = Feb-Jul), so this is not an off-by-one.

Schema-clean: keys match ForageSpecies exactly; months are integers; regions are legal RegionIds; terrain values (wetland, woodland, edge) are all legal and fit a floodplain fern; all five lookalike danger values are within the enum.

Renders safely in ForageSection.tsx — all lookalike tells display in full when the row is expanded, and lead() truncation of habitat and parts produces coherent collapsed text with no safety instruction lost.

Sustainable-harvest guidance is quantified and sourced (half of the emerged fiddleheads per crown, no second pass in the same season, only crowns with four or more fiddleheads), backed by the UMaine four-year study and Dykeman 1985.

NON-BLOCKING, recommended edit: the freezing note ends at 'blanch two minutes, ice-bath two minutes, drain and bag' without repeating that thawed fiddleheads still need the full 15-minute boil / 10-12 minute steam before eating. UMaine says so explicitly. The entry already forbids lighter cooking in the parts field, so a reader following it would still boil, but appending 'cook thawed fiddleheads fully before eating' would close the gap.

NON-BLOCKING, cosmetic: regions omit southeast even though the habitat text puts the range south to northern Virginia, and ostrich fern is native in the Virginia/West Virginia mountains. Under-inclusion is the safe direction (it never sends anyone to the wrong place) but it hides the entry, and its safety instructions, from Appalachian users.

NON-BLOCKING: lady fern is filed as 'unpalatable' while carrying thiaminase; 'toxic' would be defensible. The tell states the consequence and notes the same thorough cooking destroys it, so nothing is hidden from the reader. Conversely, cinnamon/interrupted fern is filed 'toxic' which is stronger than the evidence the tell itself describes (it says the Osmunda poisoning link is explicitly speculation) — over-caution in the safe direction.

NON-BLOCKING, cosmetic: sources are formatted 'Title - note: URL', so the renderer's /^https?:///  test fails and each source prints as a long plain string rather than a hostname link. This matches the formatting of every other entry in the file, so it is a corpus-wide styling choice, not a defect in this entry.

approvedAsIs.name: Garlic mustard
reasons: DEADLY LOOKALIKE COVERAGE IS COMPLETE. Both umbellifers that can kill someone confusing a rosette or a white-flowered top in this habitat are present: poison hemlock (Conium maculatum) and water hemlock (Cicuta maculata), both correctly marked danger:'deadly'. I actively hunted for a missing one — foxglove rosette, monkshood, fool's parsley, dame's rocket, cutleaf toothwort, fringecup/piggyback plant, violets, nettle — and found nothing deadly that belongs on the list and isn't. Cutleaf toothwort is handled in `harvest` as a conservation/native-confusion note, which is the right place for it since it is not toxic.
CAUTION LEVEL IS CORRECT. caution:'expert' matches the type contract (expert = a deadly lookalike exists) and matches reality. It is not under-rated.

THE DEADLY TELLS ARE MORPHOLOGICAL AND SEASON-ROBUST — this is the check the entry most needed to pass, and it does. Both hemlock tells rest on leaf dissection (fern-like 3–4x divided, or 2–3x pinnate with saw-toothed leaflets and veins ending in the notches) versus garlic mustard's simple kidney/heart-shaped scalloped leaf. That works on a first-year basal rosette in January as well as on a bolted plant in May, so it does not fail on the part or season actually harvested. Secondary tells (hollow purple-blotched stem, chambered tuberous root, umbel vs four-petalled cross) are correctly framed as confirmatory, and the entry explicitly says absence of purple blotching on a young hemlock proves nothing — which is the honest and correct caveat.

THE SMELL TEST IS CORRECTLY DE-RATED, WHICH IS THE FLAW I EXPECTED TO BLOCK ON. `parts` states plainly that the garlic odour fades with leaf age and after flowering, cites MSU Extension for it, and draws the right asymmetric conclusion: a strong smell is good positive evidence, a faint or absent smell is NOT evidence against — check leaf shape and the smooth/hairless surface too. Crucially, no deadly-lookalike tell depends on smell.

ROOT HARVEST IS THE HIGHEST-RISK INSTRUCTION IN THE ENTRY AND IT IS ADEQUATELY FENCED. Recommending a 'slender white taproot' in ground where poison hemlock has a white parsnip-like taproot and water hemlock has chambered tubers would normally block publication. Here it is guarded three separate times, in `parts` ('root confusion is how people actually die'), in the hemlock tell ('never dig a white taproot out of a mixed patch', with the USDA ARS fatality citation), and in the water hemlock tell ('the reason not to dig anything in wet bottomland on the assumption it is a garlic mustard taproot').

MONTHS AND REGIONS WILL NOT SEND ANYONE OUT AT THE WRONG TIME OR PLACE. months [0,1,2,3,4,5,9,10,11] read 0-indexed = Jan–Jun plus Oct–Dec, which correctly matches overwintering green rosettes plus the April–June bolt/flower window and excludes the Jul–Sep dead-and-seedy period. regions northeast/midwest/southeast sit inside the FEIS range (New England to eastern North Dakota, south to eastern Oklahoma and South Carolina).

NON-BLOCKING — TERRAIN SET IS INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT WITH THE PROSE, BUT ERRS IN THE SAFE DIRECTION. terrain includes 'upland' (per the type comment: dry rocky slopes, barrens, pine and oak scrub), which contradicts a habitat paragraph describing rich moist non-acid soil, floodplain terraces and stream banks; and it omits 'wetland' (streambanks, floodplains, damp ground) even though that is exactly the ground the habitat text describes. Since ForageSection groups species by terrain, this misplaces the entry in the browse UI. I am not blocking on it because the error runs conservative: omitting 'wetland' keeps beginners from being routed into the bottomland where both hemlocks live, and 'upland' points at dry ground with no deadly umbellifers. Worth fixing as an accuracy matter — swap 'upland' for 'wetland'.

NON-BLOCKING — regions omits 'west' although the habitat paragraph says the plant is established west of the Cascades in Washington and Oregon, and a King County WA source is cited. Under-listing a region only hides the entry from Pacific NW users; it cannot mislead anyone into harvesting somewhere hazardous. Same for the omission of month 8 (September), when fall rosettes are already up.

NON-BLOCKING — 'a brief boil or blanch with the water discarded' gives no duration. I considered this against the rule about vague instructions where a specific time is needed, and it does not rise to a block: the underlying hazard is ~100 ppm cyanide fresh weight (Cipollini & Gruner 2007), an order of magnitude below bitter almond, and mainstream sources treat garlic mustard as edible raw in normal quantities. The entry is already more conservative than standard practice and pairs the advice with a quantity caveat ('start with a small portion'). A stated '1–2 minutes' would still be an improvement.

NON-BLOCKING — one sentence in `parts` overstates the smell test as 'the tell that separates this plant from everything toxic near it'. That framing is wrong (leaf dissection is what separates it from the hemlocks), but the same paragraph immediately walks it back and no deadly tell relies on it.

NON-BLOCKING — the kidneyleaf buttercup (Ranunculus abortivus) tell degrades in the autumn/winter rosette window the entry recommends, because its non-smell fallbacks are stem leaves and flowers, neither of which a winter rosette has. I checked whether this is disqualifying and concluded it is not: R. abortivus is danger:'toxic' via protoanemonin, an acrid irritant that burns the mouth on contact and would be spat out, not a fatal exposure. Every other winter-overlapping lookalike has a smell-independent tell (golden ragwort: reddish-purple leaf underside and cobwebby hairs vs smooth and hairless; lesser celandine: glossy fleshy smooth margins and fig-shaped tubers; ground ivy: square creeping stems rooting at the nodes).

SCHEMA IS VALID. All twelve ForageSpecies fields present, months in range and de-duplicated, all region ids and terrain ids in the permitted sets, caution and every lookalikes[].danger drawn from the allowed unions, and exactly one entry named 'Garlic mustard' in the 18-entry array.

I would be comfortable with a beginner using this entry. The residual risk is concentrated in the optional root harvest, and if one change were made before publication I would make the rule explicit in `parts`: only dig a root that is still attached to a rosette you have already identified from its leaves, and never dig from a patch containing finely divided fern-like or pinnate foliage.

approvedAsIs.name: Ramps (wild leeks)
reasons: Deadly lookalike coverage is complete for the stated range. All four plants a spring ramp harvester actually meets are present: false hellebore (correctly expanded past V. viride to V. parviflorum, V. woodii and V. hybridum, which is where most guides fail), both European AND native Appalachian lily-of-the-valley (C. pseudomajalis), and fly poison (Amianthium muscitoxicum), plus trout lily as unpalatable. I looked specifically for omissions and found none that matter: eastern death camas (Stenanthium densum) is coastal-plain wet savanna, not ramp habitat, and its morphology class (strap leaves + onion-looking bulb + no onion smell) is already covered by the fly poison tell; autumn crocus (Colchicum) is a lawn/meadow garden escape and is the classic Allium ursinum confusion in Europe, not A. tricoccum in rich US woods. Arisaema and Maianthemum are not confusable at the basal-leaf stage.

The primary tell works on the part and season actually harvested. Smell-on-tear applies to a spring leaf, which is what gets picked, and it is not a flower- or fruit-dependent character. The entry goes further than most: it explicitly kills the two folk tells that get people poisoned — 'pleated leaves on one stout stalk' (true only of V. viride; V. parviflorum, V. woodii and V. hybridum all come up as separate basal leaves exactly like ramps) and 'red-purple leaf base' (Penn State records greenish-white ramp stems; A. burdickii is pale). The cross-contamination warning — sniff with clean hands, because after crushing a few ramps your fingers, knife and bag make a hellebore leaf smell of onion — is the single most important practical caveat on the smell test and it is stated. A habitat-independent second check (plump white bulb vs. Veratrum's fibrous rhizome vs. Convallaria's creeping rhizome) is given for anyone whose sense of smell is unreliable.

caution: 'expert' is correct — three deadly lookalikes. lookalikes[].danger values ('deadly' x3, 'unpalatable') are all in the enum. Schema conformance verified programmatically: all required ForageSpecies fields present, no extra keys, every lookalike has name/danger/tell, regions and terrain values are all legal.

months [2,3,4] = March-May (0-indexed) is right and matches the entry's own harvest window (shoot stage 1 Mar-15 Apr, peak leaf/bulb 15 Apr-30 May). No off-by-one. regions northeast/southeast/midwest matches A. tricoccum's range; the habitat text correctly narrows 'southeast' to the Appalachian highlands rather than the coastal plain or Deep South lowlands, which is the distinction that would otherwise send a Georgia reader to the wrong place.

No required safety preparation is omitted — ramps need none, and the entry does not imply otherwise. Harvest guidance is specific rather than vague where specificity matters: named quantities (5% harvest ~2.5 yr recovery, 10% per decade as a ceiling not a target, 0-8% max annual, no more than 1 plant in 10, Quebec's 50 bulbs / 200 g cap), a named timing rule (wait ~30 days after emergence), and the legal prohibition in Great Smoky Mountains NP with the citation.

NON-BLOCKING FIX (the one real flaw): terrain includes 'upland', which the type defines as 'dry rocky slopes, barrens, pine and oak scrub'. Ramps need rich, moist cove forest near seeps and drainages — the entry's own habitat field says 'moist', 'spring seeps, drainages and bottomland', and 'in Maine it is rich, usually alluvial hardwood forest'. The tag looks like it came from the vernacular 'rich upland forest' phrasing used inside the habitat text, not the schema's sense. Since ForageSection.tsx groups species under each terrain, ramps currently file under 'Dry slopes & barrens' alongside shagbark hickory and acorns, sending a reader to ground where ramps do not grow and fly poison does (dry oak woods, low pinelands, sandhills). I am not blocking on it because the consequence is a wasted walk rather than a poisoning — the deciding tell is smell, which is explicitly stated to be habitat-independent, and the habitat prose corrects the tag in its first clause. Recommend replacing 'upland' with 'wetland' (streambanks, floodplains, damp ground), which is what the habitat text actually describes.

MINOR, no action needed: regions omits 'southcentral' even though the entry's own Veratrum woodii note reaches OK and A. tricoccum has marginal AR/OK records. Under-claiming range is the safe direction of error — it withholds an invitation to forage rather than issuing a bad one — so I would leave it unless the range is being tightened elsewhere.
